name: Harold Boulton
bio: Harold Edwin Boulton (1859-1935), a Balliol undergraduate from 1878 who edited Waifs and Strays, in which Wilde published two poems, and who wrote the words of 'The Skye Boat Song'. He succeeded his father as second baronet in 1918. Four of Wilde's letters to him survive from his Oxford years, and the first of them is a complaint that he has not written and that he seems to prefer somebody else's company.
bio_note: Added 2026-08-05, per Lovelle. CONNECTED 2026-08-06 as attraction-expressed, arrow from Wilde - see the edge for the full reasoning and for what argues against it. It had been left flagged-not-decided, which became untenable once jealousy was accepted as an assertion of attraction on [[omero]]. STILL OPEN TO DEMOTION, and the cooling-off below is the argument for it. Original note follows. this is the strongest candidate for an attraction-expressed line among everything added today, and the call is his. WHAT WOULD SUPPORT ONE: the letter below is pique, and pique is a tell - 'I really never expected to hear from you again', the reproach about music making him 'forget everybody else', and above all the italicised comparison, that Boulton likes another young man 'MUCH BETTER than yours truly'. Wilde is twenty-three and italicising his own jealousy. WHAT ARGUES AGAINST: undergraduate friendships ran hot in this idiom generally, the 'Sir John' is a named contemporary rather than a rival in any stated sense, and the other three letters are unread. FOUR LETTERS at repo PDF 93, 110, 111 and 144; ONE read at the page (printed 66, folio confirmed, 2026-08-05). THE OTHER THREE HAVE NOW BEEN READ (in the OCR mirror, 2026-08-05; not quoted here, since nothing in them warranted an at-page verification) AND THEY WEAKEN THE CASE. Both December 1879 letters are London social management: 'I very often have beautiful people to tea'; 'I was very sorry you did not come to tea as I could have introduced you to some very beautiful people. Mrs Langtry and Lady Lonsdale and a lot of clever beings'; an offer of a bed after the theatre 'in this untidy and romantic house'; an invitation to call on his mother. The beautiful people named are all women, the address has cooled from 'My dear Harold' to 'Dear Harold', and the fourth letter is of the same kind. SO THE CASE RESTS ENTIRELY ON THE SINGLE 1878 LETTER, which is what a reader should know before deciding. It does not get corroboration from the rest of the correspondence; it gets a cooling-off. DATES 1859-1935 from the editors' note at printed 66. The context engagement that held this letter was removed 2026-08-06 when the connection was drawn - the evidence now lives once, on the edge.
